This modest, almost throwaway-sounding proverb carries real weight elsewhere in Scripture — James 4:13-15 develops the same idea at length, suggesting it struck later writers as worth expanding rather than merely repeating.

chapters.title: A Friend's Wounds, An Enemy's Kisses
chapters.teaser: Friendship is redefined by willingness to cause discomfort for someone's actual good.
body: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (v6). Pleasantness and trustworthiness are deliberately decoupled — the person who tells you something painful but true may be the one actually on your side.

This complicates any simple reading of kindness as always being agreeable — the proverb suggests real friendship sometimes looks and feels uncomfortable, while flattery, however pleasant, can mask hostile intent.

chapters.title: Iron Sharpens Iron
chapters.teaser: One of the book's most quoted images pictures friendship as mutual abrasion that improves both parties.
body: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (v17). Sharpening requires friction — the image doesn't describe passive comfort, but an active, sometimes uncomfortable process that leaves both parties better for it.

This pairs naturally with verse 6's wounds-of-a-friend proverb — together they build a picture of friendship defined less by ease and more by a willingness to challenge, refine, and be refined in turn.

chapters.title: A Reflection in Water
chapters.teaser: An unusually philosophical proverb suggests people recognize themselves reflected in others.
body: "As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man" (v19). Unlike most of the book's practical, action-oriented sayings, this one makes a quieter observation about shared human interiority.

The image suggests self-knowledge and knowledge of others aren't fully separate projects — seeing clearly into another person's heart can reveal something about your own, the way a reflection shows you your own face by way of the water in front of you.

chapters.title: Ending on the Farm
chapters.teaser: The chapter closes not with a grand principle but with practical advice about managing flocks.
body: "Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds" (v23) opens a run of verses (23-27) about attentive, ongoing management of ordinary agricultural resources.

This deliberately unglamorous ending suggests wisdom's natural home isn't abstraction but daily, attentive stewardship of whatever's actually been entrusted to you — a fitting close for a book so consistently grounded in the practical and the everyday.

chapters.title: Guilty Flight, Righteous Boldness
chapters.teaser: Fear and courage are traced to inner moral state rather than external circumstance.
body: "The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion" (v1). Nothing external is chasing the wicked in this image — the fear comes entirely from within, while the righteous stand unafraid regardless of what's actually happening around them.

This locates courage as a byproduct of a clear conscience rather than of circumstance or bravado — safety and danger measured less by what's actually threatening and more by what a person carries inside themselves.

chapters.title: Political Chaos as Moral Symptom
chapters.teaser: Rapid turnover of rulers is diagnosed as evidence of a land's wrongdoing, not simple bad luck.
body: "For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged" (v2). Governmental instability is treated as a consequence, not a random misfortune.

The implied cure is equally direct — a leader with genuine understanding extends a state's stability, tying good governance not to strategy or force but to wisdom and knowledge as the actual load-bearing qualities.

chapters.title: Cruelty From Someone Who Should Know Better
chapters.teaser: A poor man who oppresses other poor people receives one of the chapter's sharpest condemnations.
body: "A poor man that oppresseth the poor is like a sweeping rain which leaveth no food" (v3). The particular cruelty singled out here isn't wealth exploiting poverty — it's poverty exploiting itself, someone who should understand the cost inflicting it anyway.
The storm image reinforces the point: rain should nourish crops, but a "sweeping rain" destroys them instead — an image of something that should help becoming, through misuse, uniquely destructive.

chapters.title: Confession Over Concealment
chapters.teaser: Naming wrongdoing openly is treated as the actual path to relief, not the risk it appears to be.
body: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (v13). Concealment is framed as the losing strategy, despite how safe it might feel in the moment.

Notice the verse requires both halves — confession and forsaking. Naming a wrong without changing course isn't enough; mercy is tied to the combination of honest admission and genuine departure from what was admitted.

chapters.title: The Danger of Moving Fast
chapters.teaser: Speed itself is flagged as a moral red flag when it comes to acquiring wealth.
body: "He that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent" (v20), repeated with variation at verse 22. Legitimate gain, in this book's worldview, accumulates gradually — sudden wealth is treated with automatic suspicion.

This isn't a claim that all quick success is illegitimate, but a pattern-based warning: haste toward riches correlates strongly enough with cut corners and exploitation that the proverb treats speed itself as evidence worth questioning.

chapters.title: A Long Pattern, A Sudden End
chapters.teaser: Collapse is described coming not from one mistake but from repeated, accumulated refusal of correction.
body: "He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy" (v1). The emphasis on "often reproved" and "suddenly" together matters — the ending is abrupt, but the pattern behind it was long and repeatedly ignored.

This warns against mistaking gradual, unaddressed refusal of feedback for stability. What looks like a stable pattern of getting away with something can be quietly building toward a breaking point with no possibility of recovery once it arrives.

chapters.title: A Nation's Mood Set by Its Ruler
chapters.teaser: Public wellbeing is tied directly to the character of whoever holds authority.
body: "When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn" (v2). Leadership's effects aren't confined to policy outcomes — they're described shaping the emotional tenor of an entire community.

This reflects a consistent theme across the book's political proverbs: rulers aren't judged merely by competence, but by how their character ripples outward into the lived experience of everyone under their authority.

chapters.title: Perishing Without Vision
chapters.teaser: A frequently quoted line likely refers to prophetic guidance rather than ambition or imagination.
body: "Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he" (v18). Paired directly with keeping the law, "vision" here most likely means received prophetic instruction — without it, a people drift into disorder.

The verse is often applied today to organizational purpose or personal ambition, but its original context ties disorder specifically to the absence of guidance from beyond human planning alone — a people untethered from received wisdom losing their bearings.

chapters.title: The Snare of Caring What People Think
chapters.teaser: Two competing objects of trust are set against each other — public opinion and God.
body: "The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe" (v25). Social anxiety is described using the same trap imagery the book uses elsewhere for temptation and sin.

The contrast is sharp: one form of trust is explicitly named a snare, the other explicitly named safety — a stark framing of how much weight to give other people's opinions versus a deeper, steadier confidence.

chapters.title: Correction, Not Just Harshness
chapters.teaser: Absence of guidance, not severity, is what the chapter frames as the real parenting danger.
body: "The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame" (v15). The proverb pairs the rod with reproof — physical and verbal correction together — against the specific alternative of simply being left alone.

The danger named isn't strictness; it's abandonment of the correcting role altogether. Read alongside chapter 13 and 19's discipline proverbs, this reinforces a consistent claim: unchecked freedom, not firm guidance, is presented as the greater risk to a child's formation.

chapters.title: An Unusual Confession of Ignorance
chapters.teaser: Agur opens by disclaiming wisdom entirely, unlike the confident voice found through most of the book.
body: "Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man" (v2). This humility stands out sharply against the assured tone of the preceding twenty-nine chapters, closer in spirit to Ecclesiastes' uncertainty.

Whether genuine self-assessment or a rhetorical device to set up what follows, the confession reframes the chapter's authority — not another list of confident instructions, but reflections offered from someone explicitly admitting the limits of his own understanding.

chapters.title: Questions No One Can Answer
chapters.teaser: A string of rhetorical questions about divine transcendence establishes the gap between human and divine knowledge.
body: "Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment?" (v4). Each image describes an impossible feat, deliberately unanswerable by any human.

The final question — "what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?" — pushes the mystery even further, a line later Jewish and Christian readers alike have found tantalizingly open to further reflection.

chapters.title: A Prayer for the Middle
chapters.teaser: A rare direct prayer asks not for blessing but for a specific, deliberately modest amount.
body: "Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me" (v8). Unlike much of the book's confident instruction, this is a personal request — and it asks for moderation rather than abundance.

The reasoning follows immediately: too much risks forgetting God ("who is the LORD?"), too little risks dishonoring him through desperate theft (v9). Both extremes, in Agur's view, threaten the same underlying relationship, just from opposite directions.

chapters.title: Counting Up to Four
chapters.teaser: A distinct poetic form builds toward a climactic final item across several numbered lists.
body: The "three... yea, four" pattern (vv15-31) catalogs things never satisfied, things too wonderful to understand, things small yet wise, and things stately in bearing — turning simple observation of the natural world into a structured teaching device.

This numerical form appears elsewhere in the book (notably the seven abominations of chapter 6) but nowhere as extensively as here, giving chapter 30 a genuinely different poetic texture from the two-line proverbs that dominate most of the collection.

chapters.title: Small Creatures, Real Wisdom
chapters.teaser: Ants, rock hyraxes, locusts, and spiders are praised for skill despite their evident weakness.
body: "The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer; the conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks" (v25-26). Wisdom, in this list, is decoupled entirely from size or physical strength.

Locusts organize "without a king" and spiders reach "kings' palaces" through sheer persistence (v27-28) — each small creature demonstrating a different strategic virtue: foresight, habitat choice, cooperation, and tenacity, none of them requiring might to succeed.

chapters.title: A Mother's Instruction to a King
chapters.teaser: A rare passage frames statecraft as something a mother directly teaches her royal son.
body: "The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him" (v1). Almost uniquely in Scripture, this passage is explicitly framed as maternal political counsel — covering sexual discipline, sobriety, and justice for the vulnerable.

That framing matters: wisdom literature elsewhere in the book is voiced as "my son" instruction from a father, but here the authoritative teaching voice belongs entirely to the queen mother, giving her a distinct, structurally significant role.

chapters.title: Wine Judged by Who's Drinking
chapters.teaser: The same substance is forbidden to rulers and prescribed for the suffering, judged entirely by context.
body: Kings are warned off wine "lest they... pervert the judgment of the afflicted" (v4-5), while strong drink is recommended for "him that is ready to perish" so "he remember his misery no more" (v6-7).
Wine here isn't treated as inherently good or bad — its moral status depends entirely on who is drinking it and why, a nuanced position quite different from a blanket rule in either direction.

chapters.title: Speak for Those Who Cannot
chapters.teaser: The mother's political counsel culminates in a direct charge to advocate for the powerless.
body: "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction... plead the cause of the poor and needy" (v8-9). Royal power, in this framing, exists specifically to be used on behalf of those who can't advocate for themselves.

This closes the chapter's opening section on a note consistent with the rest of the book's concern for the poor — but here directed specifically at the one figure with the most capacity to actually change their circumstances: the king himself.

chapters.title: An A-to-Z Portrait
chapters.teaser: The famous "virtuous woman" poem is a complete Hebrew acrostic, each verse beginning with the next letter of the alphabet.
body: Verses 10-31 form a structured acrostic — a deliberate literary signal that this is meant as a comprehensive, alphabet-spanning portrait, not a loosely assembled list of scattered praises.

That structure is easy to miss in translation, but it shapes how the original audience would have received the poem: not spontaneous admiration, but a carefully composed, complete A-to-Z summary of what a life well lived looks like.

chapters.title: Bookending the Fear of the LORD
chapters.teaser: The book's final line returns to its opening claim, closing all thirty-one chapters on the same note.
body: "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (v30) deliberately echoes 1:7's "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge," closing the frame the book opened with.

The woman described throughout this closing poem is entrepreneurial, physically capable, and economically active — buying fields, trading textiles, planting vineyards (v14, 16, 24) — yet the poem's final verdict rests not on any of that competence, but on the same reverence the whole book has argued for from its very first chapter.
